comment: Index for the published-result pages. One entry per reproduce/<id>/ pack. Titles and summaries are plain-language and written from the pack page text; the generator checks that every id has a pack and that no id repeats. finished is the date the result was finished (YYYY-MM-DD). verdict is yes, no, unresolved or superseded. [text](finding:<id>) links to another result page.

verdict_meaning.yes: The result supports the change or claim that was tested.
verdict_meaning.no: The result does not support it, so nothing changes.
verdict_meaning.unresolved: The evidence is not strong enough either way.
verdict_meaning.superseded: A later test replaced this result.

comparisons.title: kogen-loop vs Codex
comparisons.blurb: Head-to-head tests of kogen-loop, Kogen's small stand-alone coding agent, against OpenAI's Codex command-line agent, using the same AI model at the same effort setting.

comparisons.title: Kogen vs the same agent used alone, on hard tasks
comparisons.blurb: Tests of the full Kogen product, which drives another coding agent, against that agent used on its own, on hard multi-step repository tasks.

comparisons.title: kogen-loop speed, patches and connection routes
comparisons.blurb: Small tests of changes to kogen-loop itself, and of how fast its connection to the model streams, with no second agent being compared.

comparisons.title: Test setup, rules and sandboxing
comparisons.blurb: Findings about how the tests themselves are run: written rules, changes to the test harness, and sandbox tools that confine the agent.

comparisons.title: Kogen shaping and delivery-build speed
comparisons.blurb: Measurements of Kogen's own shaping step (turning a request into an agreed specification) and of where time goes in its delivery builds. Each result tests Kogen against itself or reads recorded logs; no other agent is compared.

findings.title: kogen-loop costs less than Codex at high effort, on 14 Go tasks
findings.summary: We gave kogen-loop (Kogen's small stand-alone coding agent) and OpenAI's Codex command-line agent the same 14 fresh Go programming tasks, with the same AI model (gpt-6.1-terra) at its high reasoning-effort setting and one shared API key. A third setup let loop send the model's earlier reasoning back to it on later steps ('reasoning replay'). Every one of the 42 runs passed the task's hidden tests, which are kept private so agents cannot see them. Loop cost $0.0876 per passed task against $0.1053 for Codex, and was cheaper on 13 of the 14 tasks; a sign test (it counts on how many tasks one side won and asks whether that split could be luck) gives p=0.0018, so luck is very unlikely. Speed was tied. Reasoning replay did not help. How sure we are: fairly sure of the cost gap on short Go tasks; 14 tasks are too few to see small effects, so 'replay does not help' means 'no help seen'.

findings.title: A 'batch' tool for kogen-loop packs more work per request but does not cut cost
findings.summary: We tested a change that lets kogen-loop do several operations in one request to the model (a 'batch' tool), plus a variant that only adds a sentence asking for batching, against loop's default and against Codex. The 12 fresh Go tasks, the model (gpt-6.1-terra), the high effort setting and the API key were the same for all four setups, 48 runs in all. The batch tool did what it was built to do (2.56 operations per request against 1.74) but cost per passed task did not change ($0.1085 against $0.1101) and neither did the number of requests, so it does not advance. The sentence-only variant passed 10 of 12 tasks. Loop's default and the batch version were both cheaper than Codex on 11 of 12 tasks. How sure we are: the test could only detect large effects, so 'no change seen' is not 'identical'. This replaces an earlier four-task test ([short test](finding:batch-tool-short-test)).

findings.title: Short test of two kogen-loop 'several steps per request' tools (batch and exec)
findings.summary: An early four-task test of two changes that let kogen-loop do several operations per request: a 'batch' tool and an 'exec' tool that runs a small script. Loop's default, both changes and Codex ran on the same 4 fresh Go tasks with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra) at high effort. The batch version passed 4 of 4 at a similar cost to the default; the exec version passed only 2 of 4 and cost far more ($1.1293 per passed task against $0.1813), so exec does not advance. With only four tasks the batch result cannot be settled: the smallest chance level a four-task sign test can reach is 0.125. A larger test ([12-task confirmation](finding:batch-tool-confirm-12task)) replaced it.

findings.title: Asking the model for terser text does not change kogen-loop's cost
findings.summary: We tested whether telling the model to write less text (a 'low verbosity' setting) lowers kogen-loop's cost. The test used 3 fresh Go tasks repeated 6 times each, comparing loop with reasoning replay, the same with low verbosity, and Codex, all on the same model (gpt-6.1-terra), high effort and API key. The setting was sent and accepted, but output size and cost per passed task did not change in any reliable way, so it does not advance. Both loop setups cost less per passed task than Codex ($0.1398 and $0.1305 against $0.1868), but only 3 tasks were involved, so the page itself says the statistics overstate the evidence. One task failed in every loop run and the cause was never found.

findings.title: Adding an 'apply_patch' editing tool to kogen-loop did not reduce its output
findings.summary: We added the kind of file-editing tool Codex uses (apply_patch) to kogen-loop and compared three setups, loop's default, loop with the new tool and Codex, on 5 Go tasks run twice each (30 counted runs), with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra), high effort and API key. The tool was used and caused no errors, but the amount of text loop wrote when editing did not fall, and the model made more requests, so it does not advance. Cost per passed task is unresolved: the totals favour the new tool only because one default run ran away to the output limit and failed; without it the new tool cost 13% more. Loop's default was cheaper than Codex in 9 of 10 task blocks, though its total was higher because of that one run. How sure we are: only large effects could be detected.

findings.title: A shell that hands control back during long waits: no clear effect on hard tasks
findings.summary: On 3 hard tasks that had long command waits in an earlier test, we compared kogen-loop's default shell, a patched shell that yields control back after a bounded wait, and Codex, using the same model (gpt-6.1-terra), high effort and API key. Only 16 of the 18 planned runs finished, giving 5 complete comparisons. The yielding shell spent about a quarter of the shell time of the default and about half the wall-clock time, with equal passes (4 of 5 each; Codex 6 of 6) and equal cost, but with so few comparisons nothing is statistically significant. The default shell sat in one command until the one-hour limit both times it ran on the shell-heavy task. Unresolved.

findings.title: Sending reasoning back to the model: promising cost, but unresolved on 8 tasks
findings.summary: Eight Go tasks, three setups on the same API key and model (gpt-6.1-terra) at high effort: kogen-loop's default, kogen-loop that sends the model's earlier reasoning back to it ('reasoning replay'), and Codex. All three passed 8 of 8. Loop with replay cost $0.175 per passed task against $0.225 for the default and $0.236 for Codex, and made fewer requests, but the per-task sign tests (how many tasks one side won) could not separate the differences from chance. A larger [14-task test](finding:replayconf-14task-high) later found that replay did not help.

findings.title: kogen-loop used about twice Codex's reasoning, for the same total cost
findings.summary: Four Go tasks run twice each by kogen-loop and Codex on one API key, with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra) at high effort (and also at medium). Everything passed. At high effort loop used about twice as many reasoning tokens (27,769 against 14,106) and 1.2 times as many requests, yet the total bill was the same ($0.730 against $0.734); at medium effort loop cost $0.450 against $0.567. Why loop reasons more is not settled. Unresolved; eight runs per tool is a small sample.

findings.title: On the subscription route kogen-loop used about 40% of Codex's tokens
findings.summary: 24 Go tasks run by kogen-loop and Codex through the ChatGPT subscription route (a flat-fee login, so there is no per-request price), with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra) at medium and at high effort. All four sets of runs passed 24 of 24. Loop used about 40% of Codex's token-equivalent per passed task (38.9% at medium, 42.2% at high) and fewer on every one of the 24 tasks at both efforts. Loop's median time per run was 25-30% longer, but the two tools reached the model by different routes, so the page says the time difference cannot be blamed on the tools. The verdict covers the token result only.

findings.title: kogen-loop runs fewer shell commands than Codex in old runs
findings.summary: A read-only look at 104 earlier pairs of runs in which both kogen-loop and Codex passed the same task, at the same model (gpt-6.1-terra) and effort, to see whether loop's long runs come from extra shell work such as repeated test runs. Loop issued fewer shell commands than Codex in all 7 groups of runs and read back fewer bytes in every subscription-route group; we found no extra repeat test runs. Nothing needs changing. Two questions stay open: what the long commands on hard tasks were (their text was not kept) and whether loop's one-tool-at-a-time execution costs time. No new runs were made.

findings.title: kogen-loop's connection to the model streams as fast as Codex's
findings.summary: On the ChatGPT subscription route, we timed how fast the model's answer streams back (output tokens per second) through kogen-loop's own connection, Codex's connection and a third client, using short fixed prompts on three computers (two cloud servers and a Mac). Every tool streamed at about 40-44 tokens per second and no paired difference was significant (all p-values 0.11 or higher). The earlier reading of about 45 against 105 tokens per second did not reproduce. So there is no connection speed gap in this window. Short probes only; not a task test.

findings.title: Did kogen-loop's connection slow down on 30 October? Earlier data, now superseded
findings.summary: This analysis looked at 496 earlier runs and a few tiny probes on two Macs and found that kogen-loop's streaming speed on the subscription route fell from about 110 to about 48 tokens per second during the night, and that a direct probe pair showed loop at 45 against Codex's 81-106. A later same-computer test ([connection speed test](finding:route-same-host-throughput)) did not reproduce the probe gap, and the cause of the earlier drop was never found. Only the narrow observation that loop's speed dropped that night still stands; the page does not show it was the route.

findings.title: kogen-loop vs Codex on 8 Go tasks: cheaper at medium effort, no clear gap at high
findings.summary: kogen-loop and Codex ran 8 Go tasks on one shared API key with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra), once at medium and once at high effort. Both tools passed 8 of 8 in both settings. At medium effort loop cost 39.95% less per passed task and was cheaper on all 8 tasks (sign test p=0.0078). At high effort there was no clear difference in time or cost. The larger [14-task test](finding:replayconf-14task-high) later measured the high-effort cost gap.

findings.title: Report on whether kogen-loop is cheaper, as reliable and faster than Codex: goal not met
findings.summary: A summary of the first night of kogen-loop vs Codex testing on the same model and effort. On the clean API route at high effort loop was slower (median 139.76 s against 117.40 s) at equal pass rate and cost; at medium effort it cost 20.5% less per passed task, with a 4% lower median time but a worse slowest-tenth. On the subscription route loop's cost was 50-58% lower at tied pass rates, but the time gaps were mixed up with a speed change on the provider side and are not read as differences between the tools. The study's goal (cheaper, as reliable and faster) was therefore not met on that night's evidence.

findings.title: Three speed patches for kogen-loop: none faster or cheaper beyond noise
findings.summary: A short screening test of three changes to kogen-loop against its faster baseline build, run on a second computer with both sides on the same API key. All 16 runs passed, and no patch was faster or cheaper by more than run-to-run noise, so none was adopted. Total spend was $1.76 against a $3.00 limit.

findings.title: Letting kogen-loop's file-writing tool carry a follow-up check: not used by the model
findings.summary: We changed kogen-loop's write-file tool so that a write could carry a test command the agent already knew it would run next, saving one request. In a short test of 8 runs over 3 tasks, all passed, but the model used the new option in 0 of 3 runs where it could, so the saving was never exercised and the change does not advance.

findings.title: No faster route to the model was reachable with kogen-loop's own login
findings.summary: Using kogen-loop's own ChatGPT login and an honest client name, we tried plain HTTP with loop's usual blank client name, plain HTTP with an honest name, and a WebSocket. Every variant that answered streamed at about 54 tokens per second. The ChatGPT Codex backend refused loop's login outright (HTTP 401). So there is no route change to propose; the open question is one of eligibility, for OpenAI. No Codex arm and no coding tasks were involved.

findings.title: Choosing hard tasks for Kogen against Codex alone
findings.summary: This result selects the hard task set for comparing the full Kogen product, driving Codex, with Codex used alone: 9 tasks on which Codex at high effort had failed at least once in earlier records (success rates from 0 of 1 up to 3 of 7). The comparison itself was set up but its short test runs were not finished when this was written, so there is no outcome yet.

findings.title: Kogen driving Codex vs Codex alone, 9 hard tasks, one laptop: tied on success
findings.summary: One run per task and setup on 9 hard repository tasks. Both Kogen (driving Codex) and Codex alone passed the same 3 tasks and failed the same 6, so success did not differ (3 of 9 is 0.33; the 95% interval, which is the range the true rate could plausibly be in, is 0.12 to 0.65). Kogen took 2.6 times as long where both times were recorded. Usage and cost were not measured. Note: a later [grading correction](finding:hard-tasks-grading-correction) says the grader, not the agents, decided some of these ties.

findings.title: Kogen driving Codex vs Codex alone, 6 hard tasks, one MacBook: tied on success
findings.summary: One run per task and setup on 6 hard repository tasks. Each setup passed 2 of 6 (0.33; 95% interval 0.10 to 0.70), but not the same two: only Kogen passed two of the tasks and only Codex alone passed the other two. Kogen took 4.9 times as long on the 5 tasks where both times were recorded. Usage and cost were not measured. See also the [grading correction](finding:hard-tasks-grading-correction).

findings.title: Kogen driving Claude Code vs Claude Code alone, 6 hard tasks, one MacBook
findings.summary: One run per task and setup on 6 hard repository tasks. Kogen driving Claude Code passed 2 of 6 and Claude Code alone passed 3 of 6; the one task that differed was a Kogen timeout, so success did not differ in a way we can trust. Kogen cost 1.9 times as much at list prices ($24.99 against $13.40 in total) and took 1.4 times as long. See also the [grading correction](finding:hard-tasks-grading-correction).

findings.title: Kogen driving Claude Code vs Claude Code alone, 6 hard tasks, one MacBook, second block
findings.summary: A second set of runs on 6 hard repository tasks, one run per task and setup. Both setups passed the same 2 of 6 and failed the same 4. Where both could be priced (5 tasks), Kogen cost 3.2 times as much at list prices ($7.50 against $2.33) and, over all six, took 1.4 times as long. See also the [grading correction](finding:hard-tasks-grading-correction).

findings.title: Kogen driving Claude Code vs Claude Code alone, 9 hard tasks, one laptop
findings.summary: One run per task and setup on 9 hard repository tasks. Both setups passed the same 5 and failed the same 4 (5 of 9 is 0.56; 95% interval 0.27 to 0.81), so there was no difference in success. Kogen cost 2.4 times as much at list prices ($15.30 against $6.31 in total) and took 1.7 times as long. See also the [grading correction](finding:hard-tasks-grading-correction).

findings.title: A newer Kogen driving Codex vs Codex alone: tied on the tasks that could be graded
findings.summary: A repeat of the [earlier one-laptop test](finding:hk3-lm-hard-tasks) with a newer Kogen version, one run per task and setup. On the 5 tasks whose grading worked, both setups passed the same 3 and failed the same 2 (0.60; 95% interval 0.23 to 0.88). Kogen took 5.4 times as long (7,614 s against 1,408 s), used fewer input tokens and more output tokens. Four of the nine tasks (8 of 18 runs) are not scored because the grading was defective for them.

findings.title: What Kogen's independent review step did in hard-task runs
findings.summary: We counted, from the run logs of five hard-task blocks, what Kogen's separate review step did. All 31 reviews approved the work and none raised a blocking finding; twelve changed the code, and two of those changes broke the build check that follows (both were repaired by the next review). In these runs the review caught no defect that the grader sees. This is observation, not a controlled test, so the verdict is unresolved.

findings.title: Correction: how the grader affected the five hard-task results
findings.summary: A correction to five published hard-task results. The earlier pages and their data are unchanged; this page says what in them was decided by the grader rather than by the agents. On three of nine tasks a grader defect made every run lose the same acceptance checks, and on a fourth the task files were prepared on a Mac in a way that makes one test fail on Linux before anyone touches the code. Of 31 tied task pairs, 14 were forced ties of this kind. So these results say less than they first appeared to.

findings.title: Correction: three of the nine chosen hard tasks were chosen because of a grader defect
findings.summary: A correction to the published [choice of hard tasks](finding:hk2-hard-set) for Kogen against Codex alone. That page and its data are unchanged. Three of the nine tasks were picked because Codex had 'failed' them 7 or 8 times, but the grader never ran their acceptance scenarios, so every run lost the same checks. In the one earlier round we could still read, 18 of 36 runs lost every acceptance check this way. Graded again with the repaired grader, Codex alone passes one of those tasks. Six tasks stay selected on the original records, one on later evidence, and two are no longer supported.

findings.title: Rule: loop-vs-Codex time and cost are measured only on the two Linux servers
findings.summary: A written rule, not a measurement; no runs were made. Wall time and cost for kogen-loop against Codex are measured only on the two Linux benchmark servers, one run at a time with the tools interleaved per task. The Macs instead measure Kogen against the other tool used alone, on hard tasks, by success rate, and make no wall-time claim. The page records why the rule exists.

findings.title: Test harness change: install dependencies once, retry timed-out approvals
findings.summary: A change to the test harness, not a model result; no model was called. It installs a task's locked package dependencies once and restores a private copy for each run, and it defers (instead of failing) a run whose approval step hit its 120-second deadline. It does not fix a stalled snapshot step: the patched harness still refuses at the deadline and only retries. The page lists the exact patches and a model-free proof.

findings.title: Why a Kogen approval timed out: the shared 120-second deadline under heavy load
findings.summary: One test run failed with an approval timeout that named a file-staging step. Measurements show that step is quick (0.26 to 0.39 seconds for 2,373 files); the 120-second deadline is shared by task setup, build and snapshot, and a cold build alone takes 42 CPU-seconds, so on a computer with under 10% idle CPU the deadline can run out and the error names whichever step is running. This explanation is not confirmed. How Kogen should budget the deadline is a product decision outside this page.

findings.title: Four macOS sandbox tools measured against Kogen's old containment needs (historical)
findings.summary: Four macOS sandbox tools and one newer Kogen release were tested on one MacBook on 15 October 2026 against what the first version of Kogen needed: writes limited to chosen folders, secret locations unreadable, an allow-list of environment variables, every build process killed at the end, and a time limit. No language model ran. This is a historical measurement of the retired earlier Kogen's sandbox and those tool versions on that day, one computer and three repetitions per case, not a measurement of today's Kogen.

findings.title: Which of six ways to reuse or skip checks in Kogen builds could save time
findings.summary: Recorded logs of 44 Kogen delivery builds were replayed, with no language model involved, to see how much time six ideas for skipping or reusing the checks (test, format, compile and acceptance commands) could save. Only one has real headroom: reusing a passing check from before any change when a build restarts on the same starting files. That could save at most 7,059 seconds, about 30% of the time spent on those checks, and only if the reuse also compares the installed tools and environment, which the logs do not record. The other five show little or no headroom. Nothing was changed in Kogen; the result decided which idea to prototype next and which to drop.

findings.title: Where the time goes in Kogen builds and shaping sessions
findings.summary: Logs of 4,389 recorded Kogen sessions and 15 real delivery builds were read, with no new model calls, to find where wall-clock time goes. Two large pieces are not model time: the check commands take 36% of build time in the benchmark runs and 72% in the 15 real delivery builds, and the slowest 4% of shaping requests (180 seconds or more) hold 39% of all shaping request time. Repair after review, prompt growth in the builder, and builds that start with a failing check show little room. The sessions come from many Kogen versions and loads, so this ranks where a speed-up could matter and does not test any change.

findings.title: A cheaper model at medium effort could not get Kogen's shaping step accepted (7 of 78)
findings.summary: Kogen's shaping step turns a task request into a specification (an Intent) that its own checks must accept. With the cheaper gpt-6-luna model at medium effort, only 7 of 78 attempts were accepted (13 Go tasks, two repetitions, three arms). Of the 71 failures, 36 broke a fixed format rule, 12 failed on a single trailing full stop that the checks refuse, 22 were the model asking questions instead of submitting, and one was a provider refusal. The unmodified shaper already failed 21 of 26 times, so the two shaping changes tried in the other arms could not be judged. Under the current protocol this model is not usable for shaping; making the refusal messages clearer and tolerating the full stop is the next change to screen.

findings.title: A prototype that skips an already-passed starting check: safe, but small headroom
findings.summary: A prototype lets Kogen skip a starting check (a test, format or compile command run before any change) when the identical check already passed on the same files, command, tool versions, dependency lock files and environment. It is off by default, and any earlier failure of the same key stops reuse. It passed all 15 controls that must not reuse and the control that must, and did not hide a failure caused by the environment. Replayed over recorded builds, it would fire on about a third of starting checks and skip up to 3,094 seconds (27% of the time of restarted builds), but only four reuses reach five minutes, and the logs lack the environment details, so real savings are lower. No language model was run.

findings.title: What kogen-loop does when the model stream or its shell misbehaves
findings.summary: A fake model server injected faults into kogen-loop, with no real model call, to record how it reacts. Receiving response headers does not count as a first byte, so a stalled attempt wastes 90 seconds and three stalled attempts end at about 280 seconds. The stream is stopped after 180 seconds without progress, and keep-alive comments or half-sent events do not count as progress. A 429 reply's Retry-After value is ignored (fixed waits of 2 and 8 seconds). An unreadable event gets one immediate retry. Five productive controls, including a slow shell and a silent 700-second command, were never stopped by mistake, and a hung shell runs until the task deadline and leaves nothing behind. Nothing was changed; the result decides which behaviours are worth screening.

findings.title: Starting tool calls while the model is still streaming does not make kogen-loop faster
findings.summary: Two kogen-loop builds identical except that one starts each tool call as soon as it is fully streamed and the other waits for the response to end were run on 12 Go tasks, three repetitions each, with gpt-6.1-terra at high effort. Wall time was 16 wins for the overlapping build and 20 for the other, and the average ratio was 1.004, so the ceiling for this idea is negligible: only 0.11 seconds of tool time per run was hidden behind streaming. All 108 counted runs passed grading. In the same run both builds were slower than Codex CLI at equal pass rate (wall ratio 1.11) but cheaper per passing run ($0.0877 against $0.1090).

findings.title: Three shaping changes screened: the second-host half was invalid, the valid half shows no gain
findings.summary: Three changes to Kogen's shaping step were screened against the unchanged step on 13 Go tasks, two repetitions, 104 shapes, with gpt-6.1-terra at medium effort. Only the 40 shapes run on the Linux host are a valid measurement: specifications were accepted in 9, 10, 10 and 9 of 10 shapes (unchanged, then each change), and the share of the task's requirements they covered was .284, .285, .263 and .267, with no change showing a gain on the five tasks that could be compared per task. The other 64 shapes ran on builds missing a file the installer writes, so every one failed to start; an earlier version of this page counted them as failures, which was a test-setup fault and not a property of Kogen. A clean rerun of the unchanged shaper against one different change is in [shape-screen-s5](finding:shape-screen-s5).

findings.title: A clearer refusal message for shaping changed nothing: both versions accepted 25 of 26
findings.summary: One change to Kogen's shaping step, naming a harmless cause such as an unclosed quote or a trailing full stop in a refusal message and relaxing no rule, was screened against the unchanged step on 13 Go tasks, two repetitions, 52 shapes, with gpt-6.1-terra at medium effort. The specification was accepted in 25 of 26 shapes in both versions, and the one unequal pair was the same task failing on different repetitions with no tool call, so nothing was left for the change to fix. Average time per shape was 165 against 158 seconds. This clean run also shows that the low acceptance rate in [the earlier three-change screen](finding:shape-screen-terra-b) came from a test-setup fault. The change was dropped.

findings.title: Allowing only one resubmission broke Kogen's shaping step; allowing five matched the default
findings.summary: Kogen's shaping step lets the model resubmit a refused Intent. On an older Kogen build, with gpt-6.1-sol at low effort on 8 tasks and 6 repetitions each, the default accepted 47 of 48 shapes. Limiting resubmission to one accepted only 6 of 48, because 42 ended refused or with questions. Allowing five accepted 46 of 48 and its graded numbers were within noise of the default, about two minutes quicker per paired shape. The run is descriptive (no decision rule), so neither limit changes anything; one task cannot separate the lanes at all because its reference check always fails.

findings.title: Adding review probes to Kogen lost two net tasks on 13 Go tasks, so the patch was dropped
findings.summary: A patch adding review probes to Kogen was compared with unpatched Kogen, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task. On 13 Go tasks the hidden checks passed on 11 tasks without the patch and 9 with it: the patch gained one task and lost three, against a keep rule of at least three net wins. Cost stayed within 1.5 times. On 6 Rails feature tasks no graded pair differed and grading was incomplete, but the best case adds one win, so the verdict stands.

findings.title: One extra instruction sentence made kogen-loop about 17% faster at the same pass rate
findings.summary: Three one-sentence additions to kogen-loop's default instructions were each tested against the unchanged loop on 12 Go tasks with the same model and effort. Telling the agent to call finish right away once its checks pass cut wall time by about 17% and cost by about 20% over two repetitions (21 of 24 pairs faster), with every run passing in both arms. Combining checks into one command did nothing measurable, and a write-each-file-once sentence cut requests by a third but did not repeat its early wall and cost gain. All runs passed, so pass could not improve; only the stand-alone loop was tested.

findings.title: Switching on Kogen's request audit lost four net tasks on 13 Go tasks, so the patch was dropped
findings.summary: A patch that runs Kogen's request audit before shaping was compared with unpatched Kogen, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task. On 13 Go tasks the hidden checks passed on 11 tasks without the patch and 7 with it: no task gained and four were lost, against a keep rule of at least three net wins. Six of the 13 patched cells were refused at the shaping step, mostly because the shaped test lines were not in the required form.

findings.title: An unstated-requirement pass in Kogen shaping did not show a gain on the first 13 Go tasks
findings.summary: A patch adding an unstated-requirement pass to Kogen's shaping step was compared with unpatched Kogen, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task. On 13 Go tasks the hidden checks passed on 10 tasks without the patch and 9 with it: no task gained and one was lost, against a keep rule of at least three net wins. One repetition is still to finish and will be pooled with this run before the patch is kept or dropped.

findings.title: A coverage ledger in Kogen shaping did not show a gain on the first 13 Go tasks
findings.summary: A patch adding a model-free coverage ledger (a check of the request against the submitted Intent, shown to the reviewer) was compared with unpatched Kogen, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task. On 13 Go tasks the hidden checks passed on 9 tasks both without and with the patch: one task was gained, one was lost (the lost one ended with no model response during the build), against a keep rule of at least three net wins. One repetition is still to finish and will be pooled with this run before the patch is kept or dropped.

findings.title: A stop-when-checks-pass sentence in Kogen's builder prompt held the hidden result and cut effort on the first 13 Go tasks
findings.summary: A one-sentence change to Kogen's builder prompt (call finish right away when the checks pass, with no extra re-reads or polishing) was compared with unpatched Kogen, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task. On 13 Go tasks the hidden checks passed on 9 tasks without the change and 10 with it (one gained, none lost), and the patched build used less wall time or fewer tokens on 9 of 13 tasks, meeting the rule of at least 8. It is one trial on one laptop-class host, so it is a candidate to confirm at Kogen level before shipping, not a shipped change.

findings.title: Kogen's newer build with the delivered fixes did no worse than the previous build on 13 Go tasks
findings.summary: Two Kogen builds, the previous one (3e759e88) and the newer one that carries the delivered fixes and an updated Loop library (6a65bf3e), were run on the same 13 Go tasks with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task, nothing else changed. The hidden checks passed on 9 tasks with the newer build and 8 with the previous one (two gained, one lost), which is inside the noise of repeated identical runs, so it shows no gain and no regression. The newer build used about 13 percent more requests, mostly from one task that ended in a review block in both builds, and about the same wall time. It is one trial on one host; the newer build is used as the starting point for later experiments.

findings.title: Kogen's newer build matched the previous build on 13 Go tasks over three repetitions
findings.summary: Kogen's newer build (6a65bf3e) and the previous one (3e759e88) were run on the same 13 Go tasks with the same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), nothing else changed, three repetitions on two host types. The hidden checks passed on 28 of 39 task runs with the newer build and 27 of 39 with the previous one (three gained, two lost). Reading the cell logs, three of the five differing pairs come from acceptance checks written wrongly at shaping time on the previous build's side, and two from a request that leaves a case open on the newer build's side; none is a build or review failure of either build. The newer build used about the same wall time and 7 percent more requests once the one task that fails in both is left out. The newer build stays the starting point for later experiments; a larger comparison needs about four repetitions per arm.

findings.title: The stop-when-checks-pass sentence in Kogen's builder prompt lost to unpatched Kogen over two Go repetitions
findings.summary: The one-sentence change to Kogen's builder prompt (call finish right away when the checks pass) was repeated on the same 13 Go tasks on a second host and pooled with the first run. Across 26 task pairs unpatched Kogen passed the hidden checks on 20 and the patched build on 16 (one gained, five lost, net -4, against a keep rule of at least +3). In the second run alone the patched build lost three tasks to build_blocked and one to a refusal at shaping. A later reading (see the correction on this page and p5-loss-attribution) found these were caused by shaping defects that both arms share, not by the builder finishing early. Further repetitions are still running, so this can change; it is one trial per pair on two different hosts.

findings.title: An unstated-requirement pass in Kogen shaping lost to unpatched Kogen over two Go repetitions and is dropped
findings.summary: The patch that adds an unstated-requirement pass to Kogen's shaping step was compared with unpatched Kogen over two repetitions of the same 13 Go tasks (26 pairs), same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort). The hidden checks passed on 19 pairs without the patch and 17 with it: one pair gained and three lost, against a keep rule of at least three net wins, and the patched build ended build_blocked 4 times against 1. The patch is dropped. This replaces the first-repetition page.

findings.title: The finish-right-away sentence caused no early stops on two hard review tasks, but only one could show it
findings.summary: The kogen-loop sentence that tells the agent to call finish right away once its checks pass was tested against the unchanged loop on two hard Kogen review tasks, four paired runs each, same model and effort. On the first task both arms passed all four runs. On the second both arms failed all four runs on the same acceptance checks, so it could not separate them. Failures were four in each arm and no run with the sentence failed where its paired baseline run passed. Wall time was lower with the sentence in 6 of 8 pairs and cost in 4 of 8. Only one task could show an early stop, so the evidence is limited; only the stand-alone loop was tested.

findings.title: Turning on the request audit in Kogen shaping lost badly to unpatched Kogen over two Go repetitions and stays dropped
findings.summary: The patch that turns on a request audit before Kogen's shaping step was compared with unpatched Kogen over two repetitions of the same 13 Go tasks (26 pairs), same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort). The hidden checks passed on 21 pairs without the patch and 13 with it: one pair gained and nine lost, against a keep rule of at least three net wins, and the patched build was refused at shaping in 9 cells against 1. The patch stays dropped. This confirms the first-repetition page.

findings.title: A coverage ledger in Kogen shaping did not earn its keep over two Go repetitions and is dropped
findings.summary: The patch that adds a model-free coverage ledger to Kogen's shaping step was compared with unpatched Kogen over two repetitions of the same 13 Go tasks (26 pairs), same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort). The hidden checks passed on 20 pairs without the patch and 17 with it: one pair gained and four lost, against a keep rule of at least three net wins. The patch is dropped. This replaces the first-repetition page.

findings.title: The patched builder's losses were caused by defects written before it started, not by finishing early
findings.summary: This corrects the cause given for the stop-when-checks-pass result. We read every task where unpatched Kogen and the patched build differed on the hidden checks, and every build that stopped or was refused, across three repetitions of the same 13 Go tasks. All 7 patched losses trace to a defect written at the shaping step, which both arms run identically before the changed sentence is read: an acceptance example that contradicts the task's own Intent (checked by hand in each case), a refusal at shaping, a wrong test fixture, or an ambiguous request. Counting only the 28 pairs where both arms reached the build with a sound Intent, the patch has 0 wins and 1 loss (net -1) instead of the recorded net -6 over 38. Unpatched Kogen run against itself differed on the hidden result in 18% to 27% of pairs on a partial run, about the same as the patched build's 21%. Separately, the shaping step's acceptance example contradicted the Intent or request in 9 of 100 cells read. No gain from the patch is shown, and no early-finish problem either; one reader classified the cells, and the unpatched-against-itself run was partial.

findings.title: kogen-loop's latest version passes 13 of 14 tasks; its new cost is shell polling, not failures
findings.summary: We ran kogen-loop at its newest version inside Kogen (pin 1a3eb18) on 14 earlier tasks, once each, and compared every run with the same tasks at the previous version (8a2fcda). 13 of 14 passed; the one failure, a Kogen review task, fails the same way at both versions because the task's acceptance command needs environment variables the standalone sandbox does not set, so it is a task problem, not a loop one. The two long review tasks no longer hit the request-size refusal that stopped 2 of 8 earlier runs: the loop condenses older exchanges once. The new cost is polling: shell commands now return after one second with a handle, and one third of all requests (22% of cost) only check on a handle; the two review tasks cost about 80% more per run ($0.56 against $0.31) while their wall time fell by a quarter to a half. On the 12 short tasks the new version was about 9% cheaper and 24% faster. One run per task, so small differences are noise.

findings.title: An unstated-requirement-pass patch for Kogen showed no gain on six hard Rails tasks, where no run passed
findings.summary: A patch adding a unstated-requirement pass in shaping was compared with unpatched Kogen on six hard Ruby on Rails tasks, two repetitions pooled, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort). No run in either arm passed its hidden checks, so no pair differed (0 wins, 0 losses of 8 complete pairs) against a keep rule of at least three net wins; several runs stopped early or hit infrastructure limits. The patch is dropped on these tasks, and the tasks leave no room to show a gain at this model setting.

findings.title: A coverage-ledger patch for Kogen showed no gain on six hard Rails tasks, where no run passed
findings.summary: A patch adding a coverage ledger in shaping was compared with unpatched Kogen on six hard Ruby on Rails tasks, two repetitions pooled, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort). No run in either arm passed its hidden checks, so no pair differed (0 wins, 0 losses of 9 complete pairs) against a keep rule of at least three net wins; several runs stopped early or hit infrastructure limits. The patch is dropped on these tasks, and the tasks leave no room to show a gain at this model setting.

findings.title: A test-authoring paragraph in Kogen's builder prompt did not shorten builds on four Go tasks
findings.summary: A paragraph of test-authoring guidance (fast, deterministic tests that wait for readiness rather than sleep) was added to Kogen's builder prompt and compared with unpatched Kogen, same commit and model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), one trial per task. On four Go tasks the hidden checks passed on 3 tasks in both arms, but the patched build stage was at least 15% shorter on none of the four tasks (one 12% shorter, three longer), against a bar of at least 15% on at least 3 of 5. The run was on a heavily loaded host and did not measure the authored tests themselves, so it is a no-gain result, not a finding about test quality.

findings.title: kogen-loop's polling and refused-call fixes work: half the polling requests, no refused calls, no task broken
findings.summary: We ran kogen-loop with tonight's fixes (version 9e90bf5) against the version before them (1a3eb18) on the same 14 tasks, once each, with the two runs of a task side by side on one server. Requests that only check on a running shell command fell from 78 to 35 (-55%) and their cost by 34%; no shell call was refused (6 were before); no task that passed before failed, and the one failing task fails the same way in both for a task-side reason. Not shown: the new wait for a provider connection never triggered because no request met a network error. Also: on the three long tasks wall time rose by about 60%, because checking a command now waits up to 30 seconds instead of one, and one of those tasks took a longer path. One run per task, so small differences are noise.

findings.title: Kogen's new shaping example check refuses good specifications and loses 7 hidden passes in 65 shapes
findings.summary: Kogen's shaping step was given an example check (a model reads each acceptance example, derives its value from the written rules, and the gate refuses the specification if one contradicts) and compared with the version before it, same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), 13 Go tasks, 65 paired runs on three servers. The check did cut builds that stopped on a contradicting acceptance (9 to 3), but hidden passes fell from 47 to 40 of 65: in 15 shapes it ended shaping with a refusal or questions (1 before). Of the 12 pairs that lost a pass, 8 were shaping stopped by the check itself, most often because it called two equal values contradictory when they were only written in a different format (braced or unbraced JSON). The test was stopped early for that reason and the check is dropped until that fault is fixed; the other discordant pairs balance out (5 wins, 4 losses) and are ordinary run-to-run flipping.

findings.title: Updating Kogen's built-in loop to tonight's fixes removes refused shell calls but shows no gain in hidden passes (32 vs 31 of 52)
findings.summary: We gave Kogen's built-in loop (kogen-loop) tonight's fixes (version 9e90bf5: shell calls with an empty or unusable handle are accepted, and a request waits for the provider to accept connections instead of ending a stage after three quick network failures) and compared Kogen with and without them on the same 13 Go tasks, same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort) for every role, 52 paired runs over four repetitions on one server. The refused shell calls disappeared: 18 refusals in 17 builds before, none after, and no new kind of refusal appeared. Hidden-test passes did not change measurably: 32 of 52 before, 31 of 52 after (7 wins, 8 losses). All 15 pairs that changed are shaping refusals or ordinary build variance; three of the wins had a refused call in the other build but the logs cannot show that it caused the failure. The network wait was not tested because no request met a network error. About 29% of pairs flip between arms here, so a gain of a few passes would need about ten repetitions to show.

findings.title: Kogen's cold prompt-cache requests are conversation starts, and putting the testing rules first does not warm them
findings.summary: About a quarter of Kogen's model requests get no prompt-cache discount. Reading 184 earlier cells, we found they are the first request of each build and review conversation (9% of all input); every later request in a conversation reuses the one before it. The shaper's first request always reuses 4,096 tokens from other conversations because its unchanging instructions and tool definitions are long enough; the builder's and reviewer's are not. We moved the unchanging testing rules (15.7 KB) from the middle to the front of each conversation's first message and compared Kogen with and without that change on the same 13 Go tasks, same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort) for every role, 32 paired runs on three servers. It did nothing for caching: none of 58 lever first requests reused anything, even right after another conversation had sent the same front, and shaping stayed at exactly 4,096 tokens. Hidden-test passes were 19 and 17 of 26 graded pairs, all differences shaping defects or ordinary variance. A shared cache key per role is the remaining option, but Kogen gives every conversation its own key on purpose so a reviewer never inherits builder state; that is an owner decision.

findings.title: Kogen's current main passes more hidden tests than the build before its last nine commits (31 vs 23 of 39), mostly because the example check was removed
findings.summary: We compared Kogen's current main (e6f69a1) with the build before its last nine commits (69d09e1), same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort) for every role, 13 Go tasks, 39 paired runs over three repetitions on two servers, no patch on either side. The current main is not worse: hidden-test passes were 31 of 39 against 23 of 39 (9 wins, 1 loss), and shaping refusals fell from 8 to 1. Reading each older run's own logs, five of the nine wins are cells where shaping ended at the approval-time example check that the newer build removed (one of them only partly: the check used two of three attempts). The probe, loop and test changes explain none of the pairs, which only says these 39 runs rarely met the faults they fix. The other four wins and the one loss match no listed change and are ordinary run-to-run flipping. 13 tasks repeated three times are not 39 independent tasks, so the sign test (p = 0.021) is descriptive.

findings.title: High reasoning effort for Kogen's shaper passes no more hidden tests than medium (57 of 78 each)
findings.summary: We ran Kogen's current main twice per task, once with the shaper at high reasoning effort and once at medium, same model, with build and review at medium in both. Across 13 Go tasks and 78 paired runs, hidden-test passes were 57 of 78 on both sides, with 7 wins and 7 losses for high effort. Six of the 14 differing pairs came from the shaping stage (3 won, 3 lost); the other eight were runs that landed in both arms where one hidden test flipped (4 won, 4 lost). Fewer runs ended on a contradicted acceptance with high effort (3 against 6), but those cases split evenly and did not change the pass rate, and no new kind of refusal appeared. High effort made shaping a little slower and used more reasoning tokens, which we report only as description. Thirteen tasks repeated six times are not 78 independent tasks, so we read this as no measurable gain and keep medium.

findings.title: kogen-loop waiting up to 45 seconds for a shell command removes result-fetching requests on hard tasks
findings.summary: We let kogen-loop wait up to 45 seconds for a new shell command to finish (instead of 1 second) before handing back a handle, and compared it with unchanged kogen-loop main (166ec7f) on two hard Kogen review tasks, three runs each, the two runs side by side on one server. Requests that only fetch a shell result fell from 16 to 0, all requests fell 30% (fewer in 5 of 5 complete pairs) and wall time fell 24%; no pair changed its hidden result (one task passes 3 of 3 on both sides, the other fails on both for a task-side reason). One pair was lost to a provider error on the unchanged side and is left out. A screen on two tasks, not a confirmation.

findings.title: Letting Kogen's loop wait 45 seconds for shell commands passes the same hidden tests (55 of 78 each) and saves no requests on these tasks
findings.summary: We ran Kogen's current main twice per task, once as released and once with its loop changed so a new shell command waits up to 45 seconds for the result instead of 1 second before handing back a handle, same model and effort on both sides. Across 13 Go tasks and 78 paired runs, hidden-test passes were 55 of 78 on both sides, with 6 wins and 6 losses for the change. Requests that only fetch a shell result fell from 9 to 0, but all requests per run did not fall (15.1 against 15.7) and wall time was the same. The change altered what happened in only 10 of the 78 pairs, because only two of the tasks run commands long enough to matter, and none of those were among the 12 pairs with a different result: eight of those traced to a different shaping draw, one to a provider outage and three to a single hidden test flipping on identical builds. So this check shows no gain and no harm, and cannot say more. The earlier loop-level gain on two hard tasks is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

findings.title: kogen-loop handing small repositories to the model up front removes its look-around requests
findings.summary: We let kogen-loop add the repository listing and every small file (up to 4096 bytes, only when the listing has at most 64 paths and the shown content stays under 32 KiB) to the first request, and compared it with the same loop without it (166ec7f plus the bounded shell wait) on 14 Go tasks, two runs each, side by side on one server. Requests that only list, search or read before the first edit fell 64% (66 to 24), and to 0 on all 22 small-task runs; all requests fell 28%, and where the snapshot was sent input tokens fell 22% and output tokens 11%. No pair changed its hidden result; one pair was lost to a provider error on the unchanged side. Large repositories get no snapshot and did not change. A screen, not a confirmation.

findings.title: Handing small repositories to kogen-loop up front still removes its look-around requests on three servers, with input flat on the Mac
findings.summary: We repeated the earlier screen of kogen-loop adding the repository listing and every small file to its first request, unchanged, on a second Linux server and on a Mac, and added the three together: 14 Go tasks, two runs each, 79 scored pairs of 84 assigned (one lost to a provider error, four not run on the Mac, which hit its time cap). Requests that only list, search or read before the first edit fell 67% (190 to 63), and to 0 on all 65 small-task runs; all requests fell 26%; hidden results were identical in every pair (74 of 79 on both sides). Where the snapshot was sent, input tokens fell 11.8% and output tokens 6.2% overall, but on the Mac input was flat (+0.9%), because every Mac run spends extra rounds after its first edit. The earlier plan to join the snapshot to the loop stands. Kogen's own builder does not use this path.

findings.title: Showing Kogen's builder a small repository's files in its first request cuts its reading steps to zero and build requests by 17%, but passed no more hidden tests (57 of 66 against 58)
findings.summary: We ran Kogen's current main twice per task, once as released and once with the opening request to its builder also carrying the contents of every small file in a small repository, same model and effort on both sides. Across 11 Go tasks and 66 paired runs, the builder's reading steps before its first edit went from 70 to 0 and build requests per run fell from 4.4 to 3.7 (lower in 44 pairs, higher in 8), with no new kind of failure. But hidden-test passes were 57 of 66 against 58 for Kogen as released, with 3 wins and 4 losses for the change, and three of the four losses were one task, where the same hidden test failed in all six runs with the snapshot and in three of six without it (too few runs to tell that from chance). Tokens per run rose about 3%, because the snapshot is carried in every build request, and wall time did not clearly change. Hidden passes are the main measure and the only task that moved went the wrong way, so Kogen's builder does not take this change. The same idea inside kogen-loop's own session, which Kogen's builder does not use, is a separate result.

findings.title: Kogen's shaper on Claude Opus 5.5 through Claude Code could not be judged: the test stopped after 47 pairs ran with both arms, too few to tell
findings.summary: We ran Kogen with its shaper (the step that writes the Intent and the acceptance tests) on Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort through Claude Code, and compared it with Kogen's default shaper (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort), same build and review models, on 13 Go tasks. The test stopped early: the Claude seat hit its usage limit, and the hill climb then moved to another target. Only 47 pairs ran with both arms (34 on a busy Mac Studio, 13 on three quiet Linux servers) out of the 130 the sizing called for. Hidden passes were 15 against 14 of 34 on the Studio (8 wins, 7 losses) and 10 against 9 of 13 on the Linux servers (1 win, 0 losses), which cannot separate the two. Six Opus cells that ended on the seat limit are left out together with their pairs. Where the Opus shaper ran on quiet servers it landed 13 of 13 cells with no refusals, and nearly all of its roughly ten minutes of shaping was model time, not commands. On the busy Studio the same cells spent far more time in commands and 10 of 11 timeouts were at high load. The default shaper's refusals at its example check (10 Studio cells, 2 Linux cells) were the one shaping difference, and four of the six pairs it explains are one task that did not repeat on Linux. The two arms differ in model and in executor, so only success is compared, not speed or cost.

findings.title: Kogen's data-stores change was refused at shaping in 4 of 4 account-cleanup runs, so its coverage is unmeasured
findings.summary: We compared Kogen with its new data-stores change (816b0b0, which asks the shaper to find every store keyed by an entity's id and scope it or record a sourced decision) against the build one commit earlier (514dab4), same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort) for every role, no patch. On the account-cleanup task built for it, the new build was refused at shaping in all four paired runs because the shaper answered without calling any tool three times, while the earlier build shaped a valid intent in all four (paired sign test p = 0.0625). The new check never ran, so whether it makes the shaper cover the missed stores is unresolved. Five other tasks run once each showed no new kind of refusal, but they mostly stopped at questions in both builds, so they say nothing about build regressions. Four pairs on one task is a screen, not a rate; the refusals need a larger matched run before anyone concludes the change causes them.

findings.title: Current Kogen passed every hidden check in 1 of 18 runs on six Rails tasks, and shaped a valid intent in 8
findings.summary: We ran Kogen as it is today (514dab4, no patch) on six Rails tasks, given only the request text, with gpt-6.1-terra at medium effort for every step: three runs per task, one on each of three servers. Eight of the 18 runs wrote a valid intent, five landed a build, and one passed every hidden check. Seven stopped to ask questions nobody answered, three were refused at shaping (the shaper answered without calling a tool three times), and three builds were blocked after the first acceptance pass failed. Two tasks never reached a build in any of their three runs. Where a build landed, review approved it every time, including the four that missed hidden checks. This is the baseline for later shaping changes, not a comparison: with three runs per task and a 18 to 27 % chance that a rerun flips a result, a per-task rate means little yet. More Studio runs are queued as a follow-up.

findings.title: Kogen on Claude Opus 5.5 passed every hidden check in 1 of 12 runs on six Rails tasks, and every valid intent it shaped landed
findings.summary: We ran Kogen as it is today (514dab4, no patch) on the same six Rails tasks as the gpt-6.1-terra control, given only the request text, with Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort through Claude Code for every step: two runs per task, one on each of two servers. Four of the 12 runs wrote a valid intent, all four landed a build, and one passed every hidden check. The other eight were refused at shaping after three tries, each time because a check the shaper had written failed when Kogen re-ran it on the shaper's own example of a correct result. Review approved all four landed builds, including the three that missed hidden checks. Beside the control, this cohort passed every hidden check on a task the control never did and landed a task where the control never wrote a valid intent, while the control reached a full pass on a different task. With two runs per task and a 18 to 27 % chance that a rerun flips a result, this lists successes only and claims no model is better.

findings.title: Kogen on Claude Opus 5.5, third server: 3 of 6 runs landed a build and 1 passed every hidden check; pooled 2 of 18
findings.summary: This adds a third server to the earlier Claude Opus 5.5 check of Kogen as it is today (514dab4, no patch): the same six Rails tasks, given only the request text, with Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort for every step, one run per task. Three of the six runs wrote a valid intent, all three landed a build, and one passed every hidden check. Two were refused at shaping after three tries, because a check the shaper had written failed when Kogen re-ran it, and one stopped when the shaper asked three questions and nobody answered, which had not happened in the first 12 runs. Pooled over all 18 runs, 7 wrote a valid intent, all 7 landed, and 2 passed every hidden check, both on the same task. In the runs where the cause was logged, Kogen ran the shaper's check in a temporary copy of the project where the version manager did not trust the project's config file, a Kogen defect and not a model result. With one to three runs per task and a 18 to 27 % chance that a rerun flips a result, this lists results only and claims no model is better.

findings.title: Kogen's data-stores change was refused at shaping again on a third machine: 0 of 8 valid intents pooled, against 8 of 8 for the build before it
findings.summary: This follows up our first test of Kogen's data-stores change (816b0b0, which asks the shaper to find every store keyed by an entity's id and scope it or record a sourced decision) against the build one commit earlier (514dab4): same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort) for every role, no patch, the account-cleanup task built for the change. On a third machine the new build was refused at shaping in all 6 runs because the shaper answered without calling any tool three times, while the earlier build wrote a valid intent in all 4 clean pairs. Two more pairs had to be rerun because the earlier build's acceptance check timed out on a loaded machine; that was a machine fault, not a result. Pooled with the first test that is 0 of 8 valid intents for the new build against 8 of 8 (one-sided paired sign test p = 0.0039). The store scan still never ran, so whether the change makes the shaper cover the missed stores is unresolved; one landed build could not be graded because a clean-up job deleted its saved files first. The change has since been reverted, so this is history for the planned re-land, which will be measured the same way.

findings.title: Four more runs per task on one machine: current Kogen shaped a valid intent in 3 of 14 counted runs and passed every hidden check in none
findings.summary: This adds more runs to our baseline of Kogen as it is today (514dab4, no patch) on six Rails tasks, given only the request text, with gpt-6.1-terra at medium effort for every step, all on one Mac. We planned three more runs per task; 14 of the 18 gave a result. Three wrote a valid intent, all three reached a build, none landed, and none passed every hidden check; seven stopped to ask questions nobody answered and four were refused at shaping. Eight runs were machine faults, not results: five were refused because a fixed 120-second acceptance check timed out while the machine was heavily loaded, and three lost their process. The four timeouts of the first batch were rerun once with mixed luck, and two late reruns had not finished at the cut-off. With the earlier runs on the same machine, the six tasks have 20 results: 6 valid intents, 2 landed builds, no full pass. With four runs per task and an 18 to 27 % chance that a rerun flips a result, a per-task rate means little yet; this is the comparison base for later shaping changes on the same machine.

findings.title: A second block of Kogen on Claude Opus 5.5 passed every hidden check in 4 of 12 runs on six Rails tasks, and 11 of 12 wrote a valid intent
findings.summary: We repeated the Claude Opus 5.5 check on Kogen as it is today (514dab4, no patch): the same six Rails tasks, given only the request text, one run per task on each of two servers, with Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort through Claude Code for every step. Eleven of the 12 runs wrote a valid intent and 10 landed a build; four passed every hidden check, both runs of two tasks. Of the other two, one was refused at shaping and one ran out of its 3600 second limit in the build. Review approved all 10 landed builds. Together with the first block of 12 this makes 24 runs: 15 valid intents, 14 landed builds and 5 full hidden passes, all on two of the six tasks. The first block lost 8 runs to shaping refusals caused by a Kogen test-run setup problem; this block lost 1, and we do not know why the rate fell. With two runs per task per block and an 18 to 27 % chance that a rerun flips a result, this reports successes only and claims no model is better.

findings.title: Frozen Kogen passed every hidden check in 0 of 18 runs on six Rails tasks, and shaped a valid intent in 6
findings.summary: We ran Kogen at the frozen commit 3742abe (the same source as the earlier 514dab4 control, no patch) on six Rails tasks, given only the request text, with gpt-6.1-terra at medium effort for every step: three runs per task, one on each of three Linux machines. Six of the 18 runs wrote a valid intent, two landed a build, and none passed every hidden check. Eight stopped to ask questions nobody answered, four were refused at shaping (the shaper answered without calling a tool three times), and four builds were blocked. Pooled with the earlier control (50 runs in all) there are 17 valid intents, 7 landed builds and 1 full hidden pass. This is the baseline for the first component changes, not a comparison: with three runs per task and a 18 to 27 % chance that a rerun flips a result, a per-task rate means little yet.

findings.title: Kogen split into component modules behaved like the build before it in three matched runs
findings.summary: We compared the Kogen release before its split into separately versioned component modules (514dab4) with a plain build of the split version (573d023), same model (gpt-6.1-terra, medium effort) for every step, no patch, on three Rails tasks, one pair each, run at the same time on the same server. Two of the three pairs ended the same way (one landed a build in both, one was refused at shaping in both for the same reason), and the third stopped at different stages with the same hidden-test count (review blocked against build blocked). Neither arm passed every hidden check on any task.
